Palatable

PAL-uh-tuh-bul -- from Latin palatum, the roof of the mouth and seat of taste, the same root as 'palate.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Palatable is having a pleasant or agreeable taste.

The camp cook stirred in fresh herbs to make the bland stew more palatable for the tired hikers.

Worked Example

A school cafeteria replaces its mushy, flavorless vegetables with roasted ones seasoned with garlic, and suddenly students are actually finishing their trays.

Food pleasant enough to enjoy eating is exactly what palatable describes. Unlike 'delicious,' which promises real delight, palatable often means simply agreeable -- good enough to eat happily.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

agreeable: Agreeable means mildly pleasant and easy to accept, and it can describe weather, company, or a plan -- not just food. Palatable stays closer to the table: pleasant enough to eat or, in its figurative sense, easy enough to swallow.

tasty: Tasty means having a genuinely pleasant flavor -- food you would happily choose again. Palatable is fainter praise: it promises only that nothing about the taste puts you off. A tasty dish earns compliments; a palatable one just gets finished.

flavorful: Flavorful food is rich in taste -- bold, layered, interesting. Palatable sets a far lower bar: pleasant enough to eat without complaint. A flavorful curry excites you; a palatable one simply does not put you off.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unappetizing: unpleasant or unappealing to eat

revolting: causing strong disgust

Where it sits · how strongly the food tempts you — tolerable → palatable → appetizing

tolerable vs. palatable: Tolerable sits below palatable on this scale -- tolerable food you can force down without complaint, while palatable food is actually somewhat pleasant to eat.

appetizing vs. palatable: Appetizing is stronger than palatable: palatable food is pleasant and acceptable once you taste it, while appetizing food actively makes your mouth water before the first bite.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — palat-

root — palat-: the roof of the mouth; the seat of taste (Latin (palatum))

suffix — -able

suffix — -able: suitable for, capable of (Latin (-abilis))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin palatum named the roof of the mouth, long considered the seat of taste, and -able means 'suited to' -- so palatable food is literally 'suited to the palate,' the same root behind the English word palate itself.

Use the root in a new word: palate

Use the root in a new word: palate: Years of tasting rare spices gave the chef an unusually refined palate.

Word Choice

Palatable most often describes food that is pleasant enough to eat, but it also has a common figurative sense -- an idea or compromise can be made 'more palatable,' meaning easier to accept.
